article.articleHeadline: Recognize the Symptoms of RSV Infection in Infants, Not Just a Common Cold
article.articleSummary:
- RSV infection in infants can start like a common cold but may quickly progress to serious lower-respiratory disease such as bronchiolitis or pneumonia, as seen in Yogyakarta, Indonesia. Parents should not dismiss mild nasal symptoms in babies and toddlers. Red flags include rapid breathing: 60 breaths/min or more for under 2 months, 50 or more for 2–12 months, and 40 or more for 1–5 years, plus chest indrawing, weakness, or poor feeding. Children under two are most vulnerable, especially those under six months to one year; prematurity and congenital heart disease worsen risk. Early RSV can lead to recurrent wheeze or asthma later in life. The guidance was issued on November 19, 2026 by Amalia Setyati, a pediatric pulmonologist at Universitas Gadjah Mada (UGM).
- RSV threatens infants and toddlers in Indonesia. Dr. Amalia Setyati, a pediatric pulmonology specialist at Universitas Gadjah Mada, warns parents to recognize red flags as RSV shifts from upper to lower respiratory tract infection. Early RSV symptoms are mild, but rapid breathing is critical: 60 breaths/min or more in infants under two months; 50 in 2–12 months; 40 in 1–5 years. Other danger signs include chest retractions, weakness, and reduced feeding. The most vulnerable are under two years, especially under one year, including those under six months; prematurity and congenital heart disease raise severe risk and potential for later wheeze. Prevention options in Indonesia include maternal RSV vaccination and infant monoclonal antibodies, but costs hinder coverage in government programs.
- RSV infection poses a serious threat to the respiratory health of infants and toddlers. Often starting with mild symptoms resembling a flu or a common cold, the virus can rapidly advance to lower respiratory disease such as bronchiolitis and pneumonia, with some cases progressing to respiratory failure. Hospitalization is required in more severe cases, and intensive care may be necessary. The article cites a lecturer and pediatrician consultant respirologist at the Faculty of Medicine, Health at UGM, highlighting the need for parents to recognize alarm signs early to trigger medical assessment. As of 2026-11-19, awareness of RSV's potential severity remains crucial for early evaluation and timely care to prevent deterioration in young children.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue Virus Serotypes Detected in Reared Aedes Mosquitoes in Mataram
article.articleSummary: Detection of dengue virus RNA in lab-reared Aedes aegypti from field-collected larvae/eggs in Mataram City, Indonesia, Nov 2024–Jan 2025. Five of eight neighborhoods tested positive; DENV-3 most common (in three locations); DENV-2 and DENV-3 co-circulated in two locations; DENV-1 and DENV-4 not detected. 364 clinically confirmed dengue cases in Mataram in 2024; West Pagutan had the highest incidence. Surveillance followed WHO entomological guidelines; adult female mosquitoes were tested in pools of 20 via RT-PCR with serotype-specific primers. The study demonstrates active dengue transmission and supports targeted vector control via fine-scale neighborhood mapping; limitations include sample size and geographic coverage. This finding underscores urban arbovirus transmission risk in Mataram and the importance of vector-focused interventions.

article.articleHeadline: As of mid-November 2026, TB cases in Blora have reached 1,602 patients.
article.articleSummary: Tuberculosis (TB) in Blora Regency totaled 1,602 laboratory-confirmed cases as of 12 November 2026, according to Dinkesda Blora. This represents 89.49% of the annual case-finding target of 1,790. A total of 10,594 people were classified as TB suspects, exceeding the 2026 surveillance target of 8,700. Anton Suwoto, head of the Prevention and Control of Diseases (P3) at Dinkesda, said case finding continues, with some suspects testing positive and others negative. TB can affect all ages, from infants to adults, underscoring the importance of Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination since infancy to protect against severe TB in children. Transmission risk is not confined to urban or rural areas and is influenced by housing conditions; unhealthy homes—earth floors, poor lighting, and inadequate ventilation—raise exposure risk. The update emphasizes ongoing detection and mitigation through vaccination and improving living conditions.

article.articleHeadline: This Old Town Walking Tour Unfolds the Drama From Batavia Canal to the Malaria Outbreak.
article.articleSummary: Malaria outbreaks in Jakarta trace to Batavia's historic canal system, originally built to improve transport in the heart of the city. In Kota Tua (Old Town Jakarta), the canals created mosquito habitats that contributed to a malaria outbreak, explained by tour guide Gilang Ramadhan of the Kota Tua Jakarta Heritage Management Unit during free guided walks. The narrative uses this urban-planning lesson to discuss tropical-city resilience and climate change, noting parts of Jakarta are now below sea level and emphasizing low-emission, sustainable tourism. The tour also sketches cultural continuity in Glodok’s Chinese community, including a Mandarin calligrapher aged over 80, and references colonial-era events (1740, 1965) shaping the neighborhood around Petak Sembilan. The experience links history, public health, and environmental action, reinforced by Youth Climate Action Lab involvement.

article.articleHeadline: To Prevent the Spread of Foot-and-Mouth Disease (FMD), the Quarantine Office Destroys Buffalo Hides from Nepal.
article.articleSummary: On 19 November 2026, East Java's Quarantine Office destroyed two containers of dried buffalo hides imported from Nepal, totaling 56.39 tons, to prevent spread of foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) and Lumpy Skin Disease (LSD). The hides were buried at the Integrated Quarantine Installation in Jemundo Puspa Agro, Sidoarjo, East Java. This preventive disposal targets materials deemed potentially contaminated with FMD virus and LSD, illustrating Indonesia's border-control measures to avert introduction of infectious livestock diseases. No outbreak counts are reported; the action reflects import-risk management rather than domestic cases. The article highlights proactive quarantine authorities' efforts to mitigate transmission risk from imported animal products.

article.articleHeadline: Rabies Cases in Singkil on the Rise.
article.articleSummary: Rabies exposure cases in Aceh Singkil Regency, Indonesia, rose in 2026, reaching 120 incidents through October, up from 75 in 2025, per acting Health Office Chief Mursal. Dengue fever cases declined to 170 (from 213) and diarrhea to 749 (from 823). Data were presented at a coordination meeting on 18 November 2026. Key challenges include suboptimal early detection, limited human resources and facilities, vaccine hesitancy, treatment adherence issues, and weak cross-sector coordination. Regent Safriadi Oyon and officials urged strengthened prevention, highlighting TB control, expanded immunization coverage, enhanced mental-health services and care for persons with mental disorders (ODGJ), and accelerated safe sanitation. The Regent also called for community action to end open defecation, provide proper toilets, and maintain a clean environment, advocating coordinated, measurable efforts across districts and villages to achieve a healthier, safer Aceh Singkil.

article.articleHeadline: Measles is spreading in the US again, ending 26 years of elimination
article.articleSummary: Measles is spreading in the United States again, ending 26 years of elimination after PAHO/WHO said transmission persisted for at least 12 months. By Nov 12, 2026, the CDC counted 5,412 confirmed US cases, more than double 2025's 2,289 and far above 2024's 285; about 96% were unvaccinated or vaccination status unknown. Pennsylvania reported 1,589 cases this year as of Nov 17 and eight measles-linked deaths, including an unvaccinated Clinton County resident who died on Nov 18. Utah is the hardest-hit state with 536 cases (15.1 per 100,000). Nationwide, 45 states and DC have had measles. To regain elimination, the US must halt transmission for 12 consecutive months; elimination is not a trophy. Internationally, Indonesia 73,396 and Bangladesh 70,152 in the 12 months to Sept 2026; India 35,056; US 5,009 in the same window per WHO. India’s total through Sept 2026 was 28,605; vaccination coverage declined to 92.4% in 2025-2026 from 95.2% in 2019-2020.

article.articleHeadline: Leptospirosis cases in the Yogyakarta Special Region rise, early detection of zoonotic diseases strengthened.
article.articleSummary: Leptospirosis in the Yogyakarta Special Region (DIY), Indonesia, surged in 2025 to 453 cases with 38 deaths, up from 168 cases and 13 deaths in 2024; 2023 had 377 cases and 32 deaths. To strengthen early detection of zoonoses, DIY authorities are expanding community-based surveillance through the Disaster Risk Reduction Forum (FPRB), coordinated by the DIY BPBD with Kemenko PMK, under a One Health approach. Anthrax remains a concern, with 36 human cases in 2023 and 38 in 2024. The program aims to empower communities, health services, agriculture and food security agencies, and local governments to identify risk factors, monitor environments, and relay alerts promptly. A 19–20 November 2026 workshop will train about 100 cross-sector participants from FPRB, health, agriculture, puskesmas (community health centers), and BPBD to strengthen early warning and reporting of zoonoses and emerging infectious diseases.

article.articleHeadline: Indramayu Regional General Hospital Goes to Kalianyar Village, Integrated TB Tracing and Free Health Screenings Welcomed by Residents.
article.articleSummary: On 19 November 2026, Indramayu Regional General Hospital (RSUD Indramayu) led an integrated TB tracing and free health screening outreach in Kalianyar Village, Krangkeng District, Indramayu Regency. The program combines close-contact tracing, symptom screening, and early TB detection to identify cases sooner and prevent transmission within households and the community, with the aim of ensuring affected individuals begin treatment promptly. In addition to TB activities, residents received complimentary health checks, including blood pressure and blood glucose measurements, plus on-site medical consultations. Attendees included RSUD Indramayu’s Kabag Program/Hukum dan Humas, Media Heriyanto, Kuwu Syahroni Agus (village head), Dr. Megi Dwi Melinda of Puskesmas Krangkeng, and Tiara Putri from Puskesmas Krangkeng’s nutrition unit, along with dozens of residents. The initiative emphasizes early TB detection, stigma reduction, and strengthened collaboration among RSUD Indramayu, village administration, and health centers.

article.articleHeadline: Diarrheal diseases and cholera: the silent tragedy of contaminated water. | HSB Noticias.
article.articleSummary: Diarrheal diseases and cholera, including dysentery and rotavirus infections, caused tens of millions of childhood deaths in the 20th century, mainly through water- and food-borne transmission in settings with poor sanitation. Severe dehydration drives rapid mortality, potentially within 24 hours without treatment. The 20th century saw the end of the sixth cholera pandemic and the start of the seventh in 1961, originated in Indonesia with the El Tor biotype, spreading through Asia and Africa and reaching Latin America in 1991, infecting more than one million people and exposing urban infrastructure vulnerabilities. A simple intervention—oral rehydration salts (ORS; water, glucose, and electrolytes) developed in the 1970s—dramatically reduced child mortality in developing countries by enabling intestinal absorption of fluids during severe diarrheal episodes.

article.articleHeadline: Ghanaian Hospital Study Finds Intestinal Parasite Infection in Eleven
article.articleSummary: Intestinal parasitic infections were detected in 11.1% (394/3,542) of pregnant women attending antenatal care at Tamale Teaching Hospital in Northern Ghana (2021–2023), with 88.9% negative (3,148). Direct saline wet mount microscopy analyzed archived records; data capture was 97.82% from 3,621 identified. The Northern Ghana setting is described as underdeveloped with limited water, sanitation, and hygiene. Parasites include Entamoeba histolytica/dispar, Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Ascaris lumbricoides, Trichuris, hookworms, and Strongyloides. Maternal intestinal infections are linked to malnutrition, anemia, premature birth, impaired fetal development, and reduced birth weight; in severe cases, maternal-fetal death is possible. Globally about 24% are infected, with higher burdens in sub-Saharan Africa. Prior Ghanaian data show Central Region 19.3% and Ashanti 36.7%. Tamale serves five northern regions and neighboring countries, underscoring the regional relevance of antenatal parasitic surveillance.

article.articleHeadline: Study Reveals Zoonotic Knowledge Gaps and Livestock Biosecurity Practices
article.articleSummary: In Ada East District, Ghana, a concurrent mixed-methods study of 255 adults involved in small-scale livestock/poultry farming found a gap between general zoonotic awareness and disease-specific knowledge. About 66.3% met the threshold for good overall knowledge, but only 10.6% demonstrated high knowledge of Ebola virus disease (EVD) symptoms. While 85.1% recognized animal-to-human transmission and 94.1% acknowledged potential lethality, many respondents misattributed EVD to non-specific symptoms and some endorsed herbal or traditional remedies alongside modern treatments (89.4% had good treatment knowledge). Attitudes toward prevention were mixed, with 44% positive; 74.9% would accept an EVD vaccine if available. Biosecurity practices were largely favorable (86.7%) but PPE use was very low (73.7% never used PPE with animal fluids) and only 27.5% kept animals outside the home. Findings underscore integrating biomedical guidance with local beliefs to improve early detection and reporting.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola surveillance: Côte d'Ivoire makes online health registration mandatory for African travellers
article.articleSummary: Côte d'Ivoire imposes online health-registration for Ebola surveillance, mandating Ghanaian travellers visiting or transiting through the country to complete an online form at least 24 hours before arrival. article.articleHeadline: Pru-East MP links recurring typhoid cases to broken water system, calls for urgent rehabilitation
article.articleSummary: Typhoid fever driven by a broken Parambo-Sawaba water system is ravaging Pru-East, Ghana, with about 99 communities affected. MP Emmanuel Kwaku Boam told Parliament that typhoid, linked to unsafe drinking water, has escalated to intestinal perforation cases, the acutest form of typhoid. The enclave around Parambo-Sawaba includes about 50,000 residents, while the wider catchment exceeds 500,000. The health emergency dates back to 2022–2023 and persists despite other interventions. The Parambo-Sawaba Water System is non-functional, and the Community Water and Sanitation Agency (CWSA) is conducting a nationwide assessment of 98 broken-down systems to determine rehabilitation needs. The ministry will prioritize Parambo-Sawaba for reconstruction after assessment, with possible financing through the Pru East District Assembly. Boam urged urgent intervention, noting typhoid and intestinal perforation cannot wait.

article.articleHeadline: Luly Gil Warns About Dengue and Respiratory Viruses in Children.
article.articleSummary: {"description":"In Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, pediatrician Luly Gil reports widespread dengue, influenza, respiratory viruses and gastrointestinal infections in children, urging vigilance for alarm signs to prevent dengue shock. She notes circulating pathogens—dengue, influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and adenovirus—that can cause fever with changes in platelets and white blood cells, complicating differential diagnosis with dengue. Any child with fever longer than 48 hours, especially with other symptoms, should be evaluated to distinguish dengue from respiratory infections. Respiratory illnesses typically involve fever, cough, sneezing and nasal discharge; dengue often features malaise and retro-orbital pain, requiring medical assessment. Alarm signs include abdominal distension, epistaxis, hematochezia, pallor, hypotension and cold skin, signaling shock after fever subsides—often after day 3. She cites rotavirus and norovirus gastroenteritis; recommends hydration and acetaminophen. Prevention in schools includes rotavirus and influenza vaccination; dengue vaccines exist in some Latin American countries (Brazil) but not in the Dominican Republic."

article.articleHeadline: Review Details How Treponema Pallidum Breaches Retinal Barriers to Drive
article.articleSummary: Ocular syphilis is driving vision-threatening uveitis worldwide, as the global syphilis burden rises from about 8 million cases in 1990 to 14 million in 2019. Intraocular inflammation occurs in 0.6–2.7% of cases; posterior involvement (panuveitis/posterior uveitis) can cause irreversible blindness if antibiotics are delayed. Over half of uveitis specialists report increases in syphilitic uveitis across the Americas, Europe, Asia and Oceania, with rising cases among men—especially men who have sex with men and people with HIV—and expanding heterosexual and congenital infections. Prompt intravenous penicillin G or ceftriaxone achieves final vision stabilization/improvement in ~97% of eyes; delays worsen outcomes. Brazilian data show ~40% with permanent visual acuity loss after ~3 months of diagnostic delay; Netherlands and China corroborate. Treponema pallidum subspecies pallidum is a Gram-negative spirochaete lacking LPS, with two major lineages (Nichols-like and SS14-like) and widespread macrolide resistance (A2058G/A2059G in 23S rDNA), though beta-lactams remain effective early. Imaging implicates the retinal pigment epithelium, with ellipsoid zone disruption in ~61% of eyes in Brazilian cases.

article.articleHeadline: The Viral Isolated Tribe That Has Long Avoided the Outside World Suddenly Emerges from the Forest, What Does This Signify?
article.articleSummary: On 16 November 2026, dozens of Awá-Guajá, long isolated in Brazil’s Amazon, approached a Guajajara settlement in Maranhão state; sightings had begun on 15 November. The group briefly shared food (fruits and cassava) with villagers before retreating. Several members appeared very thin, with health status to be evaluated by technical teams. Brazil’s Funai activated the Contingency Plan for Contact Situations with Isolated Indigenous Peoples and established a joint coordination center with the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples and Sesai to prevent disease transmission from outsiders. Isolated communities remain highly vulnerable to influenza and other respiratory illnesses. Coapima cautions that this is not merely an inter-tribal contact event but signals broader concerns, including ongoing pressure on forest habitats that sustain Awá-Guajá livelihoods.

article.articleHeadline: A study identifies a gene that helps immune cells destroy the tuberculosis bacillus.
article.articleSummary: CREB3L1 identified as a key gene in controlling Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection in mice. Liver, not lung or spleen, contained bacterial replication starting around day 19 post-infection, revealing organ-specific immune programs. University of São Paulo researchers pinpointed CREB3L1, along with MYO7B and CYYR1, through RNA sequencing of liver and lung tissues and cross-referencing human data from latent TB cases. In monocytes, silencing CREB3L1 impaired uptake and killing of the bacillus and shifted cell death from apoptosis (protective) toward necrosis (inflammatory). The same gene was more active in blood from patients with active TB and marked pulmonary damage, suggesting a dysregulated inflammatory response rather than more effective infection control. About a quarter of the world population is estimated to have been infected with M. tuberculosis. Findings are preliminary; further work is needed to assess the gene’s therapeutic potential.

article.articleHeadline: 3 Health Workers Die As TB Cases Rise In Nasarawa
article.articleSummary: Three Nasarawa State health workers died of tuberculosis as cases rise amid drug resistance and equipment shortages. From January–November 2026, over 24,000 suspected TB cases were tested; more than 5,000 were confirmed positive and started on treatment; 500 children aged 4–14 diagnosed. 2024 TB data showed 8,190 cases with 35 deaths; 21% co-infected with HIV and 60 drug-resistant TB cases. Nasarawa LGA has the highest burden (1,846), followed by Nasarawa-Eggon (682), Obi (350), Awe (179), Wamba (178), Toto (143). The state has only one 10-bed DR-TB centre at ERCC Hospital, Alushi; PPE shortages and stigma hinder frontline work, with some patients seeking meds at night. DOT centers face capacity and budget delays; mobile GeneXpert/Truenat improve rapid testing, but supplies are insufficient. State aims to end TB by 2030, urging government funding and resources.

article.articleHeadline: Ministry of Health Now Requires Notification of Human Brucellosis
article.articleSummary: On November 17, 2026, Brazil's Ministry of Health added human brucellosis to the national list of compulsory-notification diseases, mandating that all suspected cases be reported to epidemiological surveillance. Public and private health services nationwide must notify authorities, with reports flowing into Sinan, the National Notifiable Diseases Information System. The goal is early outbreak detection and quicker public health action to interrupt transmission. Brucellosis, caused by Brucella spp., transfers from cattle, pigs, and sheep to humans and can also spread via inhalation in abattoirs or direct contact with infected animals or contaminated materials. A major foodborne route involves consumption of unpasteurized milk and derivatives and of contaminated meat served raw or undercooked. Symptoms are nonspecific: fever, weakness, fatigue, loss of appetite, body and head pains; sweating and muscle‑joint pains may occur. Diagnosis is challenging and underreported; treatment uses antibiotics per severity. People at risk include veterinarians, breeders, and slaughterhouse workers. Epidemiologist Roberto Medronho called the measure important for public health.

article.articleHeadline: Conserved Plasmodium vivax Protein Epitopes Yield High Southeast Asian
article.articleSummary: As of 2026-11-19, researchers map HLA-restricted T-cell epitopes within the Plasmodium vivax circumsporozoite protein (PvCSP), finding dense CD4+ and CD8+ epitopes in conserved amino-terminal and carboxyl-terminal regions. In Southern Thailand, 34 blood spots were sequenced (nested PCR, Illumina) and analyzed with 281 global reference sequences from Brazil and Vanuatu, aligned to Salvador I. Epitope predictions used the Immune Epitope Database against Thai HLA-A, -B, -C, -DRB1, and -DQA1/DQB1 alleles; the central repeat region harbors few CD4+ epitopes. Nine conserved residues within predicted epitopes are universally preserved across Thailand, Brazil, and Vanuatu isolates. Population coverage reaches 95.86% across Southeast Asia. The study provides a computational basis for a multi-epitope PvCSP vaccine to limit parasite immune evasion and aid Plasmodium vivax malaria elimination, noting ongoing vaccine development and malaria control challenges including hypnozoite relapse.

article.articleSummary: Rabies vaccination campaign in Campo Grande's rural areas will take place on Friday, November 20, as part of Black Awareness Day. The Municipal Health Secretariat (Sesau) will vaccinate dogs and cats in Rochedinho and Aguão districts, with two fixed vaccination sites: USF Rochedinho (Dr. Roger Buainain, Rua Guia Lopes, 262) and USF Aguão (Manuel Cordeiro, BR-080, km 35, toward Rochedo). In addition, Centro de Controle de Zoonoses (CCZ) teams will conduct door-to-door or property-to-property visits in remote rural properties and settlements, including Assentamento Conquista and Associação Sucuri. Veterinarians note vaccination is key to preventing rabies, a fatal viral disease that can be transmitted to humans via bites, scratches, or saliva. The schedule may be affected by heavy rain, with possible continuation into the weekend.

article.articleHeadline: Municipalities with High Schistosomiasis Positivity Decreased Over 46 Years
article.articleSummary: Schistosomiasis control in Alagoas, Brazil, shows sustained progress from 1977–2023 under the Schistosomiasis Control Program (PCE). Municipalities with positivity >15% declined from 66.1% in 1977–1996 to 24.6% in 1997–2007 and 3.75% in 2008–2023, while those with <5% positivity rose from 8.3% to 61.4% over the same periods. Program coverage expanded from 7.8% of the endemic area in 1977 to 80% by 2023. Attended population was stable 1997–2006 (annual percent change +1.2, p=0.352) and then declined 2007–2023 (APC −1.9, p=0.352). Despite progress, schistosomiasis remains an ongoing concern, with authors urging full regional expansion of PCE, environmental surveillance (including water collection monitoring for malacological assessment), and sanitation investments to further reduce transmission in the endemic area of northeastern Brazil.

article.articleHeadline: Graph Neural Networks Outperform Complex Attention in Structured Epidemic
article.articleSummary: Graph Neural Networks Outperform Complex Attention in Structured Epidemic forecasting. A benchmark on regional epidemic forecasting across Spain and Brazil shows that while Transformer-like self-attention helps with noisy surveillance, simple linear temporal models paired with graph neural networks can match or exceed such performance on structured data. Primary gains arise from graph convolutions capturing inter-regional mobility. The study compares persistence, Graph Convolutional RNN, and Graph WaveNet against two new architectures: Local Transformer-GCN (node-local self-attention with static GCN embeddings and cross-node fusion) and Global Transformer-GCN (unified spatio-temporal tokens with autoregressive masking, but quadratic memory). Spain uses province-level COVID-19 incidence and weekly inter-provincial travel, with 52 provinces and zero municipality pruning; Brazil spans over 5,000 municipalities from 2020–2023 with data anomalies and backlogs. Findings challenge the view that attention is universally superior for structured epidemiological forecasting.

article.articleHeadline: A penny-pinching method could revolutionize the meat industry: Are there that many infections?
article.articleSummary: Paraná, Brazil-based Biopark Innovation Center developed a low-cost processing intervention to curb Salmonella in poultry without raising production costs or compromising product quality. In laboratory and industrial tests, Salmonella presence dropped to the detection limit in chicken, effective across multiple serotypes and strains, with no signs of resistance. The exact formulation and application method remain undisclosed. Food-safety and sensory tests showed no chemical residues on washed carcasses, and no changes in appearance, odor, taste, or texture. Occupational health assessments deemed worker safety acceptable. Estimated costs: 0.52 EUR per ton for chicken and 0.65 EUR per ton for pork; a 1,000-ton-per-day poultry plant would incur about 520 EUR/day. Brazil processed 14.29 million tons of chicken and 5.66 million tons of pork last year. The method is an additive safety step, not a replacement for existing controls, and is in patent and regulatory approval stages.

article.articleHeadline: Global Toxoplasmosis Symposia Highlight Interconnected Transmission
article.articleSummary: Toxoplasma gondii infection is a One Health challenge highlighted at the VII Brazilian Symposium on Toxoplasmosis and IV International Symposium. Brazil reports about 68% human seroprevalence, congenital toxoplasmosis at 14.1 per 10,000 live births, and ~53 infant deaths annually. The parasite infects virtually all warm-blooded species; felids are definitive hosts, with oocysts spread through soil and water and transmission via meat tissue cysts and environmental exposure. The proceedings urge unified medical–veterinary–ecological surveillance, noting gaps beyond hospital notifications to foodborne and waterborne routes. European TOXOSOURCES and South American strain diversity show overlapping sylvatic cycles; North America links land-to-sea transport to California sea otters, with Type X and COUG genotypes. No licensed human or feline vaccines; a live attenuated vaccine exists for small ruminants. Candidate vaccines (SAG1, ROP18, GRA5, GRA7) face limitations; drug regimens vary in susceptibility, and child-friendly formulations are lacking. Calls for standardized veterinary diagnostics and cross-sector data governance.

article.articleHeadline: Minas Gerais completes 10 years free of classical swine fever and concludes surveillance cycle in 167 municipalities.
article.articleSummary: Minas Gerais marks a decade as a World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE)–recognized classical swine fever (PSC)–free zone, with ongoing surveillance by the Institute Mineiro de Agropecuária (IMA). In 2026, the state completed the 5th cycle of the Integrated Plan for Swine Disease Surveillance (PIVDS) across 167 strategic municipalities, training 46 professionals to apply new certification rules for Certified Reproductive Swine Breeding Farms (GRSC). Seapa reports pork exports rising from 20,000 tonnes in 2022 to 33,000 in 2025, supporting trade to 94 countries under strict sanitary standards. The surveillance comprises clinical (133 farms in 107 municipalities; >163,000 animals inspected) and serological (122 establishments in 88 municipalities; 1,875 blood samples for PSC and PRRS). August 18–20, 2025, Belo Horizonte hosted a training for 46 veterinarians on Portaria SDA/Mapa 1.358/2025, updating GRSC certification and biosafety requirements.

article.articleHeadline: Adapec reinforces surveillance against avian influenza in migratory birds in the Bananal Island region
article.articleSummary: Surveillance for avian influenza (highly pathogenic avian influenza, HPAI) ongoing in Bananal Island region, Tocantins, Brazil, from 16 to 19 November 2026. The Tocantins government, via Adapec, with Mapa and SES-TO, maps migratory bird concentration sites including Bananal Island and Formoso do Araguaia, visiting agricultural projects and key wetlands—Calumbi Lakes 1 and 2, Lago Taboca—to monitor birds, register species, and identify risk areas. Education activities in the Txiuri indigenous village accompany surveillance. HPAI is caused by H5N1 and is highly contagious among birds; human infection is rare but can occur with direct contact or contaminated environments. Any suspected avian influenza in domestic or wild birds should be reported to Adapec (in-person, 0800 000 4733) or via e-Sisbravet for investigation and response.

article.articleHeadline: Londrina's Santa Casa Bets on AI to Fight Hospital Infections
article.articleSummary: Nosocomial infections in Londrina, Brazil, are being addressed through a free event by Santa Casa de Londrina that promotes AI as an ally in preventing hospital infections and improving patient safety. Infectologist Walton Tedesco Jr. explains the initiative aims to connect health and technology professionals to develop AI-driven solutions for risk mapping, hygiene measures, antibiotic selection, and monitoring of inpatient procedures. He notes acceptable hospital infection rates range from 1% to 5%, with Santa Casa Londrina currently below state and national averages, though opportunities for improvement remain. AI could also identify risks related to the use of tubes, catheters, and other hospital access devices, reducing complications, length of stay, medication needs, and the risk of death. The event targets healthcare workers but is open to IT professionals and the public; in-person registrations are sold out, with online participation available via a provided link; an IT professional will present more specific technology applications in the hospital.

article.articleHeadline: Banvaco Advances in Defining Strains for a Bank of Antigens Against Foot-and-Mouth Disease
article.articleSummary: Banvaco (Regional Antigen Bank against Foot-and-Mouth Disease) advances in defining strains and antigen volumes for an emergency vaccine reserve, with a 18–19 November 2026 meeting in Duque de Caxias, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The multinational (Brazil, Bolivia, Ecuador, Paraguay, Uruguay) initiative aims to store antigens for rapid vaccine production during foot-and-mouth disease outbreaks, and to set timelines for laboratory contracting and biosafety-compliant storage. Countries must report chosen strains and antigen volumes to Banvaco by end of November; international bidding for the storage and vaccine-activation laboratory is planned for December, targeting a contract by March 2027. The PAHO Revolving Fund for vaccines procurement may be used to obtain discounts on vaccines and inputs. The process covers technical production/storage requirements, biosafety rules, and obligations of labs, signaling Banvaco’s shift to a strategic strain/volume definition while moving toward operational emergency response.

article.articleHeadline: Video: Children amused by fogging during dengue-control operation.
article.articleSummary: Video from Lábrea, Amazonas, Brazil, shows children near a fumacê spray vehicle during a dengue-control operation targeting Aedes aegypti, the vector for dengue, Zika, and chikungunya. The spray aims to reduce adult mosquitoes and is part of ongoing vector-control efforts about 702 kilometers from Manaus. The footage has drawn social-media attention and underscores risks of insecticide exposure. Public health guidance urges people to keep distance from the spraying vehicle and to avoid chasing or staying near the mist, especially children. Insecticide exposure can cause eye and throat irritation, coughing, and respiratory discomfort, particularly in sensitive individuals; seek health care if symptoms develop or worsen. The report notes no case counts or laboratory-confirmation details, highlighting the balance between vector-control benefits and chemical-risk concerns during dengue-control campaigns.

article.articleHeadline: Technical Guide Details the Hansen's Disease Care Pathway for Professionals in the Municipalities of Rondônia.
article.articleSummary: Porto Velho, Rondônia, Brazil—The state government released 'Linha de Cuidado da Pessoa Acometida pela Hanseníase - Rondônia', a technical guide co-developed by Agevisa/RO and Fiocruz-RJ's Health Information Laboratory. The document standardizes Hansen's disease care across the SUS, covering 52 municipalities in seven health regions, and aims to decentralize services to Primary Health Care, enable early diagnosis, prevent disabilities, and reduce stigma. Developed from workshops with SUS professionals, it translates technical norms into flowcharts that cover reception, diagnosis, treatment, and eventual physical and surgical rehabilitation, promoting continuous, patient-centered care. The guide reinforces integration across basic to high-complexity care and strengthens epidemiological surveillance to interrupt transmission. Agevisa/RO notes that Rondônia’s new-detection rate declined from 26.3 to 22.5 cases per 100,000 inhabitants between 2016 and 2025. Downloads are available on Agevisa/RO and Fiocruz platforms.

article.articleHeadline: PCR Testing Shows Malaria Prevalence Rose in Remote Peruvian Amazon
article.articleSummary: Malaria prevalence confirmed by PCR rose from 17.6% in 2021 to 26.09% in 2022 among remote indigenous communities in Peru’s Amazonas region (Río Santiago district), with Plasmodium falciparum prevalence reaching 24.19% in 2021 and 16.16% in 2022 in the Alianza Progreso settlement. A convergent parallel mixed-methods study of 514 participants paired cross-sectional surveys with qualitative interviews to assess malaria burden, healthcare access, and community perceptions. Diagnostics combined light microscopy and PCR; analyses used generalized estimating equations to account for repeated measures. Positive correlates of PCR-confirmed malaria included a history of prior malaria infection and chills. COVID-19-era emergency reallocations disrupted vector control, interrupted diagnostic supplies and antimalarial distributions, and reduced follow-up; fear and migration increased reliance on herbal remedies. Authors call for sustained surveillance, uninterrupted diagnostics and treatment access, and expanded healthcare in isolated settlements to advance malaria elimination in Peru.

article.articleHeadline: Yellow fever advances in Minas Gerais with low vaccination rates.
article.articleSummary: Yellow fever risk rises in Minas Gerais, Brazil, with 33 infected macaques and vaccination coverage at 87.5%, below the 95% target. As the December–May transmission window approaches, health authorities report 69 suspected human cases in 2026 through October, none confirmed. In 2025, 14 human cases and five deaths through June 30 occurred in southern municipalities Extrema, Pouso Alegre, and Poços de Caldas; none of the patients were vaccinated. No specific cure exists; severe cases require intensive care and carry high fatality. Macaques act as sentinels signaling virus circulation in forested areas, indicating risk to the unvaccinated. Vaccination via SUS is free: dose at 9 months, booster at 4 years; ages 5–59 require a single lifelong dose, with boosters for those only vaccinated before age 5. Travelers: vaccinate 10 days before travel and keep your vaccination card; augment protection with repellents and protective clothing in rural/wooded areas.

article.articleHeadline: Malaria Vaccine Shows 87% Efficacy in Clinical Trial
article.articleSummary: Malaria vaccine PfSPZ-LARC2 achieved 87% efficacy in a Phase 1 trial (22 participants) by preventing infection after deliberate parasite exposure. In a controlled challenge 12–16 weeks post-vaccination, all seven placebo recipients (n=7) were infected, while only two of 15 vaccine recipients developed infection. All infections were treated safely; the vaccine was safe and well tolerated. The study, presented at the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene meeting in Washington, D.C., was conducted by UW Medicine and partners as part of the IDCRC, sponsored by NIAID. Enrollment began Summer 2025. Testing occurred at UW Medicine in Seattle. The live-attenuated PfSPZ-LARC2 strain contains two genetic deletions that halt growth in the liver; the vaccine strain is from West Africa, while the challenge strain is from Brazil, testing cross-strain protection. Sanaria Inc. manufactured and advanced the vaccine.

article.articleHeadline: COVID-19 returns to raise concern in Espírito Santo, and Barra de São Francisco records new cases.
article.articleSummary: COVID-19 returns to raise concern in Espírito Santo as Barra de São Francisco records new cases. Of 29 tests, 9 were positive (≈30%). Municipal Health Secretary Wanderson Melgaço urges heightened protection for the elderly and those with chronic diseases. A first batch of rapid tests has arrived; more are planned, and a new vaccine batch is expected next week with groups and vaccination sites to be announced. An exclusive testing service operates at Vila Landinha Health Unit (near Casa do Cloro) Monday–Friday, 13:00–16:00; residents should present SUS and AMA cards. Key symptoms include fever, cough, sore throat and body aches; preventive measures: avoid crowds, wear masks, and maintain hand hygiene, with guidance shared for at-risk households. Barra de São Francisco, ~45,000 people, endured the 2020–2021 pandemic with over 250 deaths and a rapid crisis response, including a lockdown and a memorial at Bosque da Saudade.

article.articleHeadline: Fungal Infections Identified in Non-ICU Pneumonia Patients Without Classic
article.articleSummary: Hanoi, Vietnam—National Lung Hospital conducted a retrospective cohort of 188 adults with community-acquired pneumonia admitted to general wards (Dec 2024–Jul 2025). Invasive pulmonary fungal infection developed in 12.8% of patients lacking classic immunosuppression. Clinically diagnosed fungal disease occurred in 24 patients (23 pulmonary aspergillosis, 1 mucormycosis). In-hospital mortality was 33.3% among those with invasive fungal infection vs 2.4% without (P<0.001). Multivariable analysis identified three independent risk factors: respiratory viral PCR positivity at admission (adjusted OR 3.15; 95% CI 1.26–8.18), diabetes mellitus (adjusted OR 4.10; 95% CI 1.45–11.55), and peribronchial infiltration on chest CT (adjusted OR 4.70; 95% CI 1.87–12.48). Diagnoses followed adapted 2019 EORTC/MSGERC criteria. Authors urge heightened vigilance and early fungal diagnostic evaluation for non-ICU CAP patients, especially diabetics or those with admission respiratory viral PCR positivity, given substantial mortality differences.

article.articleHeadline: More than 1,500 pigs infected with African swine fever in Dong Thap Province.
article.articleSummary: More than 1,500 pigs infected with African swine fever (ASF) in Dong Thap Province, Vietnam. In the past week four farms in Phú Thành, Bình Ninh, Tân Đông and Vĩnh Hựu reported ASF, with 43 cases out of 273 pigs. Authorities culled 190 diseased animals, weighing over 10.2 tons. In 11 months, Dong Thap recorded 85 ASF outbreaks, with over 1,530 infected out of 3,078 pigs across 23 communes/wards; culling exceeded 2,700 diseased/deceased pigs weighing more than 120 tons. The province maintains over 498,000 pigs, similar to last year, but the herd has declined and prices hover around 5 million VND per 100 kg. Officials urge vaccination, strict biosecurity, isolation of new stock, traceable sourcing, hygiene, disinfection, and prompt reporting of suspected cases to contain spread. A local farm owner emphasizes vaccination and sanitation.

article.articleHeadline: Rabies Prevention: Free-roaming dogs, owners may be fined up to 2 million dong
article.articleSummary: Rabies prevention in Hanoi, Vietnam targets free-roaming dogs. Hanoi has ongoing dog rabies outbreaks, though human rabies cases have not been reported since 2023. Between 2023-2025, Hanoi recorded 14 dog rabies outbreaks across 8 wards/communes; since January 2026 to date, 8 dog rabies outbreaks in 6 communes. Rabies is a fatal viral disease transmitted mainly through dog bites or scratches; exposure can be mitigated by timely wound care, vaccination, and rabies immunoglobulin. New regulations (Decree 204/2026/ND-CP, effective Aug 1, 2026) impose fines for owners: 1-2 million dong if pets are not vaccinated against rabies, not muzzled, or not leashed in public. Another Decree (282/2025) sets fines 500k-1 million for roaming pets; 2-3 million for causing injury or property damage. Emphasizes vaccination compliance, owner responsibility, and public awareness; calls for authorities to enforce and educate at community level.

article.articleHeadline: A ploy by a group of doctors at the Institute of Pulmonology to turn 114 healthy people into cases of severe pulmonary tuberculosis.
article.articleSummary: Former Hanoi Pulmonary Hospital deputy director Doan Van Huan and accomplices allegedly forged 164 medical files for 114 people to obtain postponement of prison terms or reduced sentences. The Bac Ninh City Prosecutor’s Office charges Huan with forging records to present healthy individuals as patients with severe pulmonary tuberculosis, including multi-drug resistant TB, for bribes. The scheme involved fabricating symptoms (cough with sputum, coughing blood, fatigue, weight loss), ordering tests and chest X-rays, and swapping real TB sputum samples to create false positives. Chest X-ray results were altered to show advanced disease; some patients were staged as inpatients to bolster the records. From 2021–2025, the group reportedly earned about 1.18 billion VND. A total of 37 people are charged with using fake documents; some bought records 4–5 times.

article.articleHeadline: You can still develop pneumonia even without fever or much coughing.
article.articleSummary: Two elderly patients in Hanoi, Vietnam, demonstrate atypical pneumonia presentations. At the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, an 81-year-old man with gout, type 2 diabetes, hypertension and chronic kidney disease developed fever and severe knee pain three days before admission; on arrival he had fever, bilateral lung crackles, and tophi, with chest imaging (X-ray and CT) confirming pneumonia after initially being suspected of a gout flare. A 72-year-old woman with hypertension and diabetes reported fatigue, generalized aches, chest tightness and shortness of breath without fever; imaging and tests diagnosed pneumonia. Clinicians emphasize that in older adults, respiratory infections often lack classic symptoms due to aging-related immune decline and comorbidity burden. They caution against self-medication, advise proper nutrition and physical activity, maintaining warmth, and avoiding abrupt temperature changes; promote annual influenza vaccination and consider pneumococcal and RSV vaccines, with early medical evaluation for unusual symptoms.

article.articleHeadline: Community Trust and Risk Perception Drive Malaria Mass Drug Administration
article.articleSummary: Malaria mass drug administration (MDA) effectiveness hinges on community participation. A systematic review of 25 qualitative and mixed-methods studies (through 2026) identifies four engagement themes: perceptual/cognitive factors, individual/household dynamics, social/community interactions, and health-system/programmatic structures. Data from sub-Saharan Africa (14 studies) and the Greater Mekong Sub-Region (10 studies), with one South Asia study, show that high perceived malaria risk and trusted leadership promote participation, especially when local health workers are involved and ancillary care accompanies MDA. Barriers include fear of adverse events, potential economic disruption to daily livelihoods, rumors, and limited understanding of asymptomatic malaria. Decisions to participate reflect a social risk-benefit calculation mediated by trust in the health system. The authors urge continuous, responsive engagement and long-term partnerships with local leaders to tailor strategies and sustain elimination efforts.

article.articleHeadline: Thailand is Now the Regional Hub for Mpox as Cases Surge to 470 With Three Deaths as Clade Ib Spreads
article.articleSummary: Mpox in Thailand reached 470 confirmed infections and three deaths in 2026 through October 31, with more than 300 cases detected between mid-July and late October as Clade Ib spread. The Department of Disease Control reported these figures on November 3, 2026, amid rising concerns over ongoing transmission in Thailand, a regional tourism and travel hub. Clade Ib accounted for 54 infections between August 24 and September 6. Symptoms may be atypical, including a single blister, localized sores, swollen lymph nodes, severe throat pain, or anal inflammation; fever, headaches, myalgias, and fatigue can occur. Diagnosis relies on PCR testing of lesion samples; routine blood tests are not definitive. Incubation can reach 21 days. Most infections resolve with supportive care; pregnant women, children, and immunocompromised individuals face higher risk. Vaccination with MVA-BN is available for high-risk groups where supply allows, with isolation until lesions heal and avoidance of shared items.

article.articleHeadline: Urban Landscape Structure Shapes Bangkok Mosquito Breeding Sites Across
article.articleSummary: Bangkok, a dengue-endemic metropolis, shows Aedes aegypti breeding sites are structured by urban morphology and daily human practices. A field survey from May 2023 to December 2024 in 36 zones documented 4,921 artificial containers in public spaces, excluding natural oviposition sites. Small <1 L containers dominated the pool and drove inter-neighborhood variation, with densities from about 19 per km for sub-0.5 L receptacles to roughly 1 per km for those over 5 L. In Wat Daowaduengsaram and Victory Monument–Ramathibodi, containers >1 L comprised nearly half of local inventory. Building density plus landscape configuration explained over half the variation in container coverage, with a non-linear U-shaped pattern along Axis 1: highly compact cores and open peripheral neighborhoods harboring more containers. Vegetation configuration (Axis 3) showed no direct link to total counts, implying internal spatial arrangement matters. The study supports the Resource-Based Habitat approach to guide urban vector surveillance and control.

article.articleHeadline: Antibiotic-resistant bacteria speak out; Centre for Health Protection urges prudent use of antibiotics to prevent infections.
article.articleSummary: Hong Kong's Centre for Health Protection released a social-media video in the first-person voice of 'this bacterium' to warn that antibiotic-resistant bacteria can strike at any time, featuring survivor Mr. Gu recounting his near-fatal infection. The post emphasizes prudent antibiotic use, hand hygiene, and environmental cleanliness. It explains resistance emerges when humans overuse antibiotics, allowing bacteria to train resistance genes and survive antibiotic exposure, leading to harder-to-treat infections, longer illness, and higher death risk. Global context: antimicrobial resistance caused about 4.71 million deaths in 2021; without action, annual deaths could reach 8.22 million by 2050. In Hong Kong, from 2020–2030 there could be 18,433 deaths related to antimicrobial resistance (roughly five per day). The campaign includes a video of Mr. Gu, who recalls near-death when fever delayed treatment. Date: 2026-11-19.

China remains the fourth-highest TB burden country, accounting for 6.5% of global new cases; MDR/RR-TB in China totals 26,000 (2024), ranking third, with China, India, the Philippines, and the Russian Federation hosting over half of global MDR-TB. 2025 regional distribution of new cases: Southeast Asia 35%, Western Pacific 27%, Africa 25%, Eastern Mediterranean 8.7%, Americas 3.4%, Europe 1.7%. Global incidence declined 14% since 2015; deaths fell 35%. Only 59% of new diagnoses used rapid diagnostics; approximately 370,000 MDR-TB cases globally, with 42% treated and 6-month regimens used. China’s ‘No TB Community’ pilots seek upstream prevention, while TB research funding remains far below the target.”}

article.articleHeadline: Six months after drinking freshly squeezed goat milk, a boy developed a fever and was diagnosed with brucellosis.
article.articleSummary: In Xi’an, Shaanxi Province, a 9-year-old boy developed a 17-day fever up to 39.7°C with knee pain, later experiencing testicular discomfort. After multiple antibiotic and antiviral treatments failed, clinicians considered mumps (parotitis) and brucellosis. A key history reveal showed six months earlier, the grandfather took him home and they drank freshly squeezed raw goat milk. Blood cultures grew Brucella, confirming brucellosis; the child improved rapidly after appropriate antibiotics. The report warns that unpasteurized fresh milk carries a high Brucella infection risk, and exposure to cattle or sheep or consumption of undercooked beef/lamb can cause brucellosis. It advises seeking prompt medical evaluation for persistent fever, sweating, and migratory bone/joint pain to rule out brucellosis, rather than attributing symptoms to a common cold.

article.articleHeadline: Machine Learning Predicts Liver Fibrosis Risk in Prior Schistosoma
article.articleSummary: Schistosoma japonicum–related liver fibrosis risk predicted by machine learning in Jiangsu, China. In 6,158 individuals with documented historical infection treated with praziquantel, ultrasound-detected liver fibrosis was found in 4,314 (70.1%). Despite China’s nationwide schistosomiasis japonica transmission interruption in 2023, many treated persons remain at risk for progressive hepatic damage. Biopsy remains gold standard but is invasive; ultrasound is non-invasive but suffers inter-observer and equipment variability; serological scores for viral hepatitis poorly apply to post-schistosomiasis fibrosis. Data from the 2021–2022 Jiangsu Schistosoma japonicum Infection Cohort were analyzed; median age 64 years, 57.1% male, with exclusions for hepatitis B/C, alcohol liver disease, MAFLD, autoimmune disease, and primary hepatic cancer. article.articleHeadline: Sichuan CDC Warns That Norovirus Will Become Epidemic; Strengthening Prevention and Control Cannot Be Delayed
article.articleSummary: Norovirus outbreak warning from the Sichuan CDC calls for strengthened prevention as winter arrives. In Sichuan, November–January is the peak, with outbreaks in schools, kindergartens, and elder-care facilities. Incubation is 12–48 hours; symptoms include vomiting and diarrhea, with adults more often diarrhea and children more often vomiting. Most cases are mild and resolve in 1–3 days, but infants, the elderly, and the immunocompromised may recover more slowly; rare cases become severe. Transmission occurs via person-to-person contact, contaminated food or water, and vomit aerosolization. There is no vaccine; people remain highly susceptible, and little cross-protection exists between genogroups, enabling reinfection. Prevention emphasizes proper handwashing (seven steps with soap and running water for at least 20 seconds) and safe food/water practices (boiled water, thoroughly cooked foods, washed produce, avoiding raw shellfish). Illness requires home isolation during symptoms and for 3 days after resolution, with continued hand hygiene and limited contact with healthy household members.

article.articleHeadline: Sulfated Polysaccharides from Codonopsis pilosula Inhibit Influenza A
article.articleSummary: Influenza A virus replication is inhibited in cultured host cells by semi-synthetic sulfated derivatives of Codonopsis pilosula polysaccharides, addressing public health challenges from seasonal and pandemic influenza A (notably H1N1) and resistance to neuraminidase inhibitors and M2 blockers. article.articleHeadline: Male Partners of HPV-Positive Women Frequently Carry Shared Viral Strains
article.articleSummary: Kunming, China-based paired cross-sectional study of 303 heterosexual couples (Jan 2024–Dec 2025) found external genital HPV DNA in 149 men (49.2%), with high-risk genotypes in 121 men (39.9%). Secondary analyses showed female multi-type infection associated with male positivity (aOR 1.62, 95% CI 1.00–2.63). The cross-sectional design cannot infer transmission direction; findings support partner-focused counseling on vaccination eligibility, barrier protection, and smoking cessation.

article.articleHeadline: Salvianolic Acid C Blocks Influenza Virus Release by Targeting Viral
article.articleSummary: Salvianolic acid C, a bioactive component of Salvia miltiorrhiza, blocks influenza virus release by binding neuraminidase and impeding terminal budding, demonstrated across multiple influenza A subtypes. Identified via a stepwise framework starting from Xuebijing injection, the compound was profiled among 81 constituents, with molecular docking showing binding in the neuraminidase active site (binding energies up to −9.5 kcal/mol) and 100-ns MD simulations confirming a stable complex (RMSD ~2.1 Å after 55 ns). In vitro assays yielded CC50 >200 μM and EC50 = 9.39 μM against influenza A (SI >21.3); additionally, 8.14 μM against amantadine-resistant A/WSN/33 (H1N1), 9.86 μM against A/Hong Kong/498/97 (H3N2), and 14.87 μM against A/Chicken/Guangdong/1996 (H9N2) with SI >13–24. Broad-spectrum efficacy and low cytotoxicity suggest potential as an antiviral complement to existing neuraminidase inhibitors facing H275Y resistance. article.articleHeadline: Procalcitonin SOFA Score and CD4 Count Predict Talaromyces Marneffei Sepsis
article.articleSummary: Independent prognostic factors for AIDS complicated by Talaromyces marneffei sepsis identified as procalcitonin (PCT), SOFA score, and CD4+ T-cell count in a single-centre retrospective study at Liuzhou People's Hospital (2017 Jan–2025 Mar). Using Cox regression, researchers derived a prognostic index (PI): PI = 0.930 × PCT + 1.584 × SOFA + 1.350 × CD4+ T-cell count. The PI demonstrated strong discrimination with AUC 0.901 (95% CI 0.859–0.942), SE 0.021, sensitivity 80.0%, specificity 88.8% (P < 0.001). Based on PI, patients were categorized into low (>0–1.5, n=129), moderate (1.5–3.0, n=60), high (3.0–4.0, n=34) risk groups, showing 28-day survival of 90.7%, 38.3%, and 8.8%, respectively. The study concludes the PI provides a practical tool for short-term risk stratification and outcome assessment in Talaromyces marneffei sepsis complicating AIDS.

article.articleHeadline: Experimental mRNA Vaccine Shows Protective Efficacy Against Toxoplasma
article.articleSummary: Toxoplasma gondii infection (toxoplasmosis) is targeted by an experimental mRNA vaccine using lipid nanoparticle delivery encoding the surface antigen SRS34A. In a 19 November 2026 preclinical study from Longyan University in Fujian, China, mice mounted balanced humoral and cellular responses and showed partial protection against both acute and chronic toxoplasmosis. Vaccinated mice survived longer after lethal acute challenge with the virulent type I RH strain and exhibited markedly fewer brain cysts after chronic challenge with the type II ME49 strain. Bioinformatic analyses identified SRS34A as highly expressed across oocysts, tachyzoites, and bradyzoites and predicted to be exposed on the parasite surface, validating it as an antigen target. Current therapies (pyrimethamine+sulfadiazine) suppress tachyzoites but poorly target dormant bradyzoites and have adverse effects. A veterinary vaccine (ToxoVax) exists; no human vaccine is marketed yet.

article.articleHeadline: Beijing Tertiary Center Audits Hepatitis C Surveillance Data and Identifies
article.articleSummary: Beijing Ditan Hospital, Chaoyang District, Beijing, conducted a 2023 quality verification of hepatitis C surveillance data. article.articleHeadline: Dairy Processing Study in India Evaluates Milk Quality and Microbial Safety
article.articleSummary: Kanpur, Uttar Pradesh, India: a cooperative dairy facility processing ~150,000 L/day demonstrates that combining biochemical standardization with microbial safety surveillance preserves quality and prevents processing failures. Intake testing covered organoleptic assessment, acidity (lactic acid), fat by Gerber, solids-not-fat, and heat stability (clot-on-boiling, alcohol stability). Acidity <0.18% lactic acid suits pasteurisation; higher levels cause heat-induced coagulation and processing failure. Biochemical analyses show full-cream milk at 6.0% fat and 9.0% SNF; toned milk 3.0% fat, 8.5% SNF; butter >80% fat, moisture <16%; curd SNF ~9.5% due to fermentation concentration. Microbiological profiling enumerates total bacteria, coliforms, yeasts, molds, and lactic acid bacteria; pathogenic species detected include E. coli and Staphylococcus aureus, with molds Aspergillus and Penicillium present. Beneficial Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus support fermentation. Integrated platform-testing, finished product chemistry, and microbial surveillance enable governance of safety and consistency in large-scale dairy processing in India.

article.articleSummary: Ehrlichia canis, a globally distributed tick-borne pathogen of dogs, was analyzed using 16S rRNA sequences (n=67) from multiple regions, including 17 new sequences from India, to assess genetic diversity and population structure. Nine haplotypes were identified with low diversity (Hd = 0.302 ± 0.073); a predominant haplotype was shared across distant populations, while India showed the highest haplotype richness and Mexico higher nucleotide diversity. Negative Tajima's D and Fu and Li's F values, with a star-like haplotype network, suggest demographic expansion or neutrality departures, though selection, structure, and uneven sampling may contribute. AMOVA showed 93.23% of variation within populations, with low, non-significant differentiation (FST = 0.06765, P = 0.27664). The weak geographic structuring at the conserved locus and lack of genome-wide homogeneity or transcontinental gene flow highlight the need for balanced sampling and higher-resolution genomics to baseline E. canis population genetics.

article.articleHeadline: Zoonotic Diseases: How Inequality Drives Pandemic Risk
article.articleSummary: Zoonotic diseases cause an estimated 2.7 million deaths and 2.5 billion illnesses annually, with about 60% of known human infectious diseases and 75% of emerging infections zoonotic. Economically, COVID-19 fatalities exceed seven million; IMF global output losses reach $13.8 trillion through 2024, and around 70 million people fell into extreme poverty in 2020. Looking forward, the value of lives lost to viral epidemics could reach $22 trillion per year, while recurring pandemics may cost about $228 billion annually in lost national income. Preventive measures—such as regulating wildlife trade and reducing deforestation—cost far less than losses (less than one-twentieth). The One Health framework seeks cross-disciplinary action across human, animal, and environmental health, but remains dominated by biomedical approaches and institutional silos; it must decentralize and integrate to address structural drivers and inequalities that heighten spillover risk. About a billion poor people in Asia and Africa keep livestock, linking livelihoods to spillover risk, with vaccination gaps noted for rabies, brucellosis, bovine tuberculosis, and leptospirosis, and India showing income-related vaccination disparities.

article.articleHeadline: TB symptoms persist in 3 of 4 patients after treatment: AIIMS Patna study
article.articleSummary: In AIIMS Patna, a BMJ Open study of 256 adults within a month of completing pulmonary TB treatment found 195 (76.2%) still experienced respiratory symptoms, with cough being most common and about half reporting breathlessness on climbing stairs or walking uphill. Chest CT or spirometry abnormalities occurred in 93.4% of participants, including lung scarring and abnormal widening of airways. The study highlighted psychological impact, with elevated anxiety in 58.2% and elevated depression in 48%. These findings underscore that TB care must extend beyond medication completion to include post-treatment monitoring, mental health support, and potentially pulmonary rehabilitation. Advice includes consulting pulmonary specialists for persistent symptoms and avoiding smoking, tobacco exposure, dust, and smoke. The work was conducted under an Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) project led by Dr Dipendra Kumar Rai at AIIMS Patna.

article.articleHeadline: Monkey fever surveillance intensified in C'magaluru, Shivamogga
article.articleSummary: Kyasanur Forest Disease (KFD), or monkey fever, surveillance intensified in Chikkamagaluru and Shivamogga districts, Karnataka. In 2026, 3,098 people were tested in Chikkamagaluru; 72 tested positive (64 from Koppa, 6 NR Pura, 2 at Manipal Hospital) and all recovered. Nine monkey deaths occurred in Chikkamagaluru this year, none tested positive for KFD. KFD is tick-borne with no human-to-human transmission; the transmission season runs from November to June. Affected areas include Koppa, NR Pura, and Sringeri in Chikkamagaluru district, and Teerthahalli, Sagar, Hosanagara in Shivamogga district. Preparations are under way as cooler months favor tick proliferation due to drier leaf litter. Preventive measures include tick collection, surveillance, DEPA oil distribution, vaccination drives, repellents, and hot-water bathing after forest visits. Five fatalities were reported in Shivamogga last season, all with comorbidities. Interdepartmental coordination and review meetings are planned.

Experts from Global Tiger Forum, National One Health Mission, ICMR-National Institute of One Health, Wildlife Institute of India, and the Environment Ministry are addressing diseases affecting big cats, emerging pathogens, and cross-species transmission risks. The workshop will conclude Friday with field training at Sariska Tiger Reserve, including practical demonstrations on biological sample collection, remote biopsy of big cats, sample preservation and transport, plus post-mortem and forensic sampling in suspected hunting and poisoning cases.

article.articleHeadline: India Maps Regional Viral Outbreak Priorities to Guide Zonal Pandemic
article.articleSummary: India mapped regional viral outbreak priorities across four geographic zones (North, South, East, Central) to guide four zonal National Institutes of Virology in Jammu, Bengaluru, Dibrugarh, and Jabalpur, as part of PM Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (World Bank-supported) to address COVID-19-era gaps. A March 2024 cross-sectional study used a modified One Health Zoonotic Disease Prioritization tool with multicriteria decision analysis to rank 40 candidate viral pathogens into three groups (A: 10 common/high-priority; B: 15 limited occurrence; C: 15 rare but high-risk for emergence or import/export). Five criteria were weighted: outbreak potential 25%, disease severity 22%, introduction/transmission risk 20%, socioeconomic impact 18%, and existing prevention/control capacity 15%. The process involved 186 participants from public health, surveillance, diagnostics networks, veterinary and academic institutes, across four zones, in three phases: baseline listing, pre-workshop surveys, and two-day hybrid Delphi consensus workshops.

article.articleHeadline: Review Finds Sternoclavicular Joint Tuberculosis Diagnosed After Five
article.articleSummary: Sternoclavicular joint tuberculosis is an exceptionally rare extrapulmonary TB manifestation, representing <1% of all osteoarticular TB. A systematic review of 48 studies (1955–2024) with 117 confirmed patients found prognosis largely favorable when appropriate antituberculous chemotherapy is initiated, but diagnostic delays exceed five months due to indolent, nonspecific symptoms. The literature, English-language and database-validated up to March 1, 2025 with updates through August 5, 2025, spans five databases and regional indexes; 89.6% of studies were published after 2000, 77.08% after 2010. Case reports dominate (70.8%), case series 22.9%, and observational studies 6.3%; methodological quality averaged 45%. The pooled cohort had mean age 42.4 years (SD 17.16; range 11–90), with male predominance (63.8%). Notable historical reports include Japan (1955) and the United States (1982); recent reports come from India and Burkina Faso (2024). Lack of diagnostic consensus and standardized guidelines hampers early detection and optimal management.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue, fever cases up as mosquito menace worsens

Stagnant rainwater in unmaintained plots, overflowing stormwater drains, and discarded roadside waste sustain Aedes mosquito breeding; residents report daylong mosquitoes inside homes and near school gates, despite sporadic anti-larval spraying and delayed clearing of waterlogged pockets. Health facilities, including Govt Rajaji Hospital (GRH) and UPHCs, are seeing a steady influx of fever patients presenting for blood tests and outpatient care. To ease tertiary hospital burden, Madurai Corporation has launched daily afternoon monsoon medical camps at UPHCs and weekly Thursday vector-control drives to destroy breeding grounds in schools, colleges, and public facilities, with Domestic Breeding Checkers assisting. Officials say there is no localized outbreak; cases are scattered citywide, and higher numbers reflect broader screening rather than a surge of transmission.

article.articleHeadline: Tuberculosis Deaths Continue to Decline Worldwide
article.articleSummary: TB deaths worldwide fell to 1.13 million in 2025, a 4% decline from 1.18 million in 2024 and a 35% drop from 1.74 million in 2015, signaling sustained mortality reductions across the TB epidemic. The most pronounced progress occurred in the WHO African and European regions, where deaths were halved between 2015 and 2025, with reductions of about 50% and 51%, respectively. Outside these regions, two high-burden countries—China and India—achieved a 35% reduction by 2025, indicating notable gains outside the African/European-region trend. The article underscores ongoing global progress in tuberculosis mortality and highlights persistent regional disparities, illustrating that large declines in some regions coexist with continued burdens in others. article.articleHeadline: South Asian Avian Influenza Research Surged as Clade 2.3.4.4b Spread Across
article.articleSummary: Integrated analysis of two decades of avian influenza investigations across eight South Asian nations reveals an accelerating literature trajectory and distinct clade 2.3.4.4b transmission dynamics. From 2005–2025, Scopus-curated literature comprises 858 peer‑reviewed articles (84.85% primary research; 15.15% reviews) and 267 complete hemagglutinin sequences from the GISAID EpiFlu database, enabling phylogenetic reconstructions. Annual output rose from under 20 publications early on to peaks in 2021–2024 (57–73). India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh account for 96% of regional output (India 385 papers, 5,520 citations; Pakistan 232, 3,366; Bangladesh 210, 4,073). Leading institutions: University of Veterinary and Animal Sciences (Pakistan) 103; ICAR NIHSAD (India) 67; Chittagong Veterinary and Animal Sciences University (Bangladesh) 66 with 1,637 citations. Maldives had no indexed articles; Nepal 4.43%, Bhutan 0.93%, Sri Lanka 0.82%, Afghanistan 0.70%. The clade shows persistent local maintenance in domestic waterfowl, low-level human transmission, and cross-border connectivity, within a One Health, transboundary research shift.

article.articleHeadline: Two diseases threaten goats in winter; beware if these symptoms appear.

Keep animals in dry, clean, well-ventilated housing; avoid wet floors, which raise pneumonia risk. If symptoms appear, isolate suspected cases immediately and seek veterinary care rather than attempting home remedies. The diseases impact growth in kids and milk yield in adults, underscoring the importance of sanitation, housing, and vaccination.

article.articleSummary: Kinshasa — Kenyan Defence Forces (KDF), part of MONUSCO, bolster Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of Congo by assuming ongoing security duties in Nia Nia, Ituri, after transferring from Nepal’s rapid-response unit. The Fifth Kenyan Quick Response Force (KENQRF 5) took over two months ago as Ebola containment escalated, enabling MONUSCO to maintain civilian protection, safeguard critical infrastructure, and facilitate access to health services. The new mandate emphasizes shielding civilians, countering threats from armed groups, supporting community Ebola-prevention awareness, and securing treatment centers and essential health facilities. The deployment also aims to protect healthcare workers, aid agencies, and local communities, strengthening coordination between security and public health to ensure uninterrupted humanitarian operations amid Ebola outbreaks. Ongoing outbreak risk persists due to security and health conditions.

article.articleHeadline: Uttarakhand Government Steps Up Preparedness Over Ebola Virus Concerns
article.articleSummary: Ebola virus disease (EVD) preparedness in Uttarakhand, India, as of 19 November 2026, follows a WHO report of thousands infected across the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria. The Centre advised states to take precautionary measures; Uttarakhand has strengthened traveller surveillance, isolation facilities, and hospital readiness, with AIIMS Rishikesh designated as a dedicated isolation hospital for suspected and confirmed cases. Doon Hospital staff are screening arrivals from affected countries. Measures prioritize early identification and isolation, PPE for healthcare workers, and adherence to infection prevention protocols. Symptoms typically appear 2–21 days after exposure and begin with fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache, and sore throat, progressing to vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain and rash; severe disease can involve liver/kidney dysfunction, confusion, and bleeding. Diagnosis requires laboratory confirmation. Contacts should be monitored for 21 days and avoid direct contact with infected individuals or contaminated objects; suspected patients must be hospitalized for care.

article.articleHeadline: Gaps in Regional Legal Frameworks Threaten East Africa Bundibugyo Ebola
article.articleSummary: 6,342 confirmed Bundibugyo Ebola virus cases and 3,072 deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) as of 2 September 2026, with the outbreak beginning 15 May 2026 in Mongbwalu, Ituri Province; the WHO declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern on 17 May 2026. Uganda contained domestic transmission and declared the outbreak over within its borders, but external partners imposed unilateral travel restrictions, prompting Africa CDC to call for lifting punitive measures against transparent reporting. The authors argue that robust public health diplomacy requires binding regional legal arrangements to sustain cross-border operations under political stress, noting the IHR (2005) lacks reciprocal protections. During 2026, technical, semantic, and organizational interoperability succeeded—Africa CDC sequencing exchanges, harmonized case definitions, and Uganda–DRC coordination—yet the legal dimension remains under-institutionalized in the East African Community. A 1 June 2026 KLM flight suspension to Entebbe illustrates collateral impacts of non-evidence-based travel measures. Public health diplomacy should be permanent peacetime infrastructure to mitigate governance gaps.

article.articleHeadline: Kasaï-Oriental: nearly 790,000 malaria cases, including 694 deaths recorded in one year.
article.articleSummary: Malaria remains a major public health problem in Kasaï-Oriental, Democratic Republic of Congo. For 2025, nearly 790,000 confirmed malaria cases and 694 deaths were recorded in the province, according to the PNLP. Children under five and pregnant women are especially at risk. To fight the surge, Governor Jean-Paul Mbwebwa Kapo launched a house-to-house enumeration campaign coupled with free distribution of insecticide-treated nets (ITNs). In total, 3,194,314 nets are destined for about 1,263,241 traditional households across the province, with door-to-door distribution to reach remote communities. The PNLP representative stressed that effectiveness hinges on actual use, not just distribution. The governor urged community leaders to ensure a transparent rollout, and he personally distributed nets in targeted households to demonstrate commitment.

The aid responds to shortages reported by local Caritas Congo partners; as a member of Caritas Internationalis, Katolikus Karitász coordinated from stockpiles to meet demand. The shipment traveled via international humanitarian routes, supported by the EU Humanitarian Air Bridge and the Logistics Cluster, routing through Entebbe, Uganda to Bunia. Local Caritas Bunia director Abbé Justin Zanamuzi expressed gratitude; Katolikus Karitász director Zagyva Richárd highlighted solidarity extending beyond borders.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in Ituri: Traditional Healers Commit to Strengthening Early Warning for Suspected Cases - ACP
article.articleSummary: In Ituri province, northeastern Democratic Republic of Congo, including the city of Bunia, traditional healers commit to strengthening early warning for suspected Ebola virus disease cases. Georges Busha, newly elected president of the Ituri Provincial Council of Traditional Healers, said healers should alert competent health services if a case presents signs consistent with Ebola, and they will not treat patients. Healers can aid in community-level detection and rapid referral for medical care beyond traditional medicine’s capacity, leveraging proximity to communities. The plan includes training sessions on hygiene, best practices, and the limits of traditional medicine, with aims to unify healer associations and combat charlatanism. The initiative emphasizes closer collaboration with doctors and nurses to facilitate referrals and link suspected cases to modern health services amid Ebola concerns in Ituri.

article.articleHeadline: Gilead licenses Ebola drug for Nigeria, 126 other countries
article.articleSummary: As of 2026-11-19, Gilead Sciences has licensed obeldesivir, an investigational Ebola drug, to generic manufacturers under royalty-free voluntary agreements covering 127 countries, including Nigeria, to facilitate potential future access. Dr Anu Osinusi, Gilead’s VP for Virology, announced during the Ibadan College of Medicine Alumni Association's 2026 Alumni Day that access would depend on trial results and regulatory approvals. Obeldesivir is being studied as an oral post-exposure prophylaxis to prevent Ebola after exposure, targeted at healthcare workers, household contacts, and others at high risk. During the Democratic Republic of Congo outbreak, a WHO-supported treatment-evaluation platform and the EVO-PEP post-exposure trial were activated. Early non-human primate data suggested that combining antivirals with antibodies may improve survival, but not yet proven in humans. Osinusi urged sustained African investment in research and preparedness.

Participants were encouraged to address challenges in environmental health, focusing on changing harmful practices such as indiscriminate waste disposal, open defecation, unsafe food preparation, and improper wastewater disposal during rains.

article.articleHeadline: Why humans get the worst of Ebola virus
article.articleSummary: Ebola virus causes about 50% fatality in humans. The Democratic Republic of Congo's current outbreak has surpassed 10,500 confirmed cases and 5,130 deaths (CDC). A Cell study from the La Jolla Institute for Immunology, with Princeton and UC San Diego collaborators, identifies a key reason humans suffer more: Ebola builds viral condensates or 'nests' inside host cells, and traps certain human mRNAs inside these compartments. Trapped mRNAs include those encoding type I interferon and other antiviral defense genes (ISGs). Degradation of these mRNAs normally deactivates antiviral signaling; when trapped, the innate response stays on, driving dangerous inflammation and organ failure. Bat cells, in contrast, show different mRNA folding and mRNAs are not recruited into condensates, preventing symptomatic infection. The finding suggests a molecular basis for human susceptibility and viral pathogenesis, rooted in mRNA structure and condensate dynamics.
